items.title: Balanced maps from a right module and a left module, and bilinear maps over a commutative ring
The tensor product $M\otimes_R N$ from the additive group underlying the free $\mathbb Z$-module on $M\times N$, elementary tensors, and finite tensor sums
Universal property of the tensor product for balanced maps into abelian groups
items.strategy: Let $F=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$ be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on $M\times N$, and regard its underlying additive group explicitly as the free abelian group on that set. View the target abelian group as a $\mathbb Z$-module, extend a balanced map uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-linear map from $F$, check that it kills every generator of the relation subgroup $H$, and factor through $F/H$. Conversely compose a homomorphism out of $F/H$ with the elementary-tensor map. Prove the two assignments inverse and retain the empty and zero-module cases.

items.title: Tensor products are unique up to a unique isomorphism carrying elementary tensors to elementary tensors
items.strategy: Given two representing pairs, apply each universal property to the other's universal balanced map. Each composite fixes every elementary tensor, so uniqueness makes the composites identities. State uniqueness relative to the specified universal maps, which licenses the phrase 'the tensor product'.

items.title: Module homomorphisms induce tensor-product homomorphisms functorially
items.strategy: For a right-linear map $f:M\to M'$ and a left-linear map $g:N\to N'$, verify that $(m,n)\mapsto f(m)\otimes g(n)$ is balanced and invoke the universal property. Check identity and composition on elementary tensors, then use uniqueness; over a commutative ring record that the induced map is linear for the separately constructed module structure.

items.title: A formula on elementary tensors defines a homomorphism exactly when its underlying pairing is balanced
items.strategy: Restate the universal-property bijection as a descent test: a prescription $m\otimes n\mapsto b(m,n)$ extends precisely when $b$ is additive in each variable and balanced. Then give the mandatory failure: on $\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z$, the prescription $q(m\otimes n)=m$ would send $2\otimes1=1\otimes2$ to both $2$ and $1$, so it is not well defined. Emphasize that checking a formula only on symbols is never enough.

items.title: $(S,R)$-bimodules and commuting left and right scalar actions
A commuting outer scalar action descends to a tensor product
items.strategy: If $M$ is a right $R$-module and $N$ an $(R,S)$-bimodule, use the universal property to define $(m\otimes n)s=m\otimes(ns)$ and check the right $S$-module axioms on elementary tensors. Prove the left-handed analogue and the compatibility needed for iterated tensor products. Each equality is forced by a balanced pairing, not by an unchecked symbol rule.

items.title: Associativity of tensor products for compatible bimodules
items.strategy: For a right $R$-module $M$, an $(R,S)$-bimodule $N$, and a left $S$-module $P$, construct $(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\to M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$ from $(m,n,p)\mapsto m\otimes(n\otimes p)$. Build the reverse map similarly. Prove both maps are defined through successive universal properties and check the composites on elementary tensors.

items.title: Over a commutative ring, $M\otimes_RN$ is an $R$-module with $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$
items.strategy: Keep this separate from the arbitrary-ring construction. For fixed $r$, descend $(m,n)\mapsto(rm)\otimes n$ through the universal property, use commutativity to verify balance, and check the module axioms on elementary tensors. The defining balance relation proves equality with $m\otimes(rn)$. Note explicitly that no such single $R$-action is asserted for an arbitrary noncommutative ring.

items.title: Symmetry and associativity isomorphisms for tensor products over a commutative ring
items.strategy: Descend $(m,n)\mapsto n\otimes m$ to obtain the symmetry isomorphism and make its square the identity by checking elementary tensors. Specialize balanced associativity to commutative-ring modules, verify $R$-linearity using the constructed module action, and state naturality of both isomorphisms.

items.title: The regular module is a tensor unit: $R\otimes_RN\cong N$ and $M\otimes_RR\cong M$
items.strategy: Send $r\otimes n$ to $rn$ and $m\otimes r$ to $mr$; balance makes both maps well defined. Their inverses send $n$ to $1\otimes n$ and $m$ to $m\otimes1$. Check both composites on elementary tensors and use the unit laws, including the zero ring and zero modules.

items.title: Finite iterated tensor products represent multilinear maps independently of parenthesization
items.strategy: Induct on the number of factors using the binary universal property and associativity. Take the empty tensor product to be $R$ and the one-factor tensor product to be the module itself; verify those two boundaries separately. Use the associativity isomorphisms to transport the representing map between parenthesizations and uniqueness to prove coherence for the comparison used here.

items.title: Tensor products commute with arbitrary direct sums
items.strategy: For an arbitrary family $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ over a commutative ring, construct the map from $(\bigoplus_iM_i)\otimes_RN$ by summing the coordinate tensor maps; finite support makes the sum legitimate. Construct the inverse from the family of maps $M_i\otimes_RN\to(\bigoplus_iM_i)\otimes_RN$. Use the two universal properties and check both composites on summands and elementary tensors. Include $I=\varnothing$.

items.title: The elementary tensors of two bases form the product basis of the tensor product
items.strategy: Identify free modules on basis sets $I$ and $J$ with direct sums of copies of $R$. Apply arbitrary direct-sum distributivity twice and the tensor-unit isomorphism to obtain $R^{(I)}\otimes_RR^{(J)}\cong R^{(I\times J)}$. Track the canonical generators to show that the resulting basis is exactly $(e_i\otimes f_j)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$, including either empty basis.

items.title: $R^m\otimes_RR^n\cong R^{mn}$ with the product basis, and $\dim_F(V\otimes_FW)=\dim_FV\,\dim_FW$
items.strategy: Apply the product-basis theorem to the standard bases indexed by $m$ and $n$, and identify the product index set with $mn$. Over a field, apply this to finite bases of $V$ and $W$ and the published definition of dimension. Check $m=0$ or $n=0$ explicitly: both sides are the zero module and the product basis is empty.

items.title: The $R$-module $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ over a commutative ring
For finite-dimensional $V$, the canonical map $V^*\otimes_FW\to\operatorname{Hom}_F(V,W)$ is an isomorphism
items.strategy: Use evaluation to descend $(\phi,w)\mapsto[v\mapsto\phi(v)w]$. Choose a finite basis of $V$ with dual basis and send $T$ to the finite sum of dual-basis tensors with $T$ of the corresponding basis vectors. Check the two composites on basis vectors and elementary tensors; treat $V=0$ by the empty sum.

items.title: Under $\operatorname{End}_F(V)\cong V^*\otimes_FV$, tensor contraction is the trace
items.strategy: For a finite basis and its dual, identify a rank-one tensor $\phi\otimes v$ with the endomorphism $x\mapsto\phi(x)v$. Its matrix has trace $\phi(v)$. Extend linearly and use the finite-dimensional Hom-tensor isomorphism; verify the zero-dimensional case gives the zero map and trace zero.

items.title: Algebras over a commutative ring, central structure maps, and algebra homomorphisms
The tensor product of $R$-algebras has multiplication $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$
items.strategy: For algebras whose commutative base ring acts centrally, use the finite multilinear universal property to descend the four-variable multiplication formula, and separately descend $r\mapsto r(1\otimes1)$ for the structure map. Verify associativity, distributivity, and the identity $1\otimes1$ on elementary tensors; if both factors are commutative, so is the result. The descent guard supplies well-definedness before any ring-law computation.

items.title: Universal mapping property of the tensor product of commutative algebras
items.strategy: For $R$-algebra maps $f:A\to C$ and $g:B\to C$ with $C$ commutative, the pairing $(a,b)\mapsto f(a)g(b)$ is bilinear, so it induces $A\otimes_RB\to C$. Check multiplicativity and the identity on elementary tensors. Conversely any algebra map compatible with $a\mapsto a\otimes1$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$ is forced on $a\otimes b=(a\otimes1)(1\otimes b)$, proving uniqueness.

items.title: Hom-tensor adjunction: $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M\otimes_RN,P)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P))$
items.strategy: Send $F$ to the curried map $m\mapsto[n\mapsto F(m\otimes n)]$ and reverse the construction by uncurrying an $R$-linear map into Hom. Verify additivity, balance, and $R$-linearity explicitly before applying the tensor universal property. Check the two constructions inverse on evaluations and state naturality in all three modules.

items.title: Tensoring is right exact
items.strategy: For an exact sequence $A\to B\to C\to0$ and a module $N$ over a commutative ring, prove surjectivity on elementary tensors by lifting their first factors. Quotient $B\otimes_RN$ by the image from $A\otimes_RN$ and construct the inverse map from $C\otimes_RN$ using a lift of $c$; exactness makes the value independent of the lift. The descent guard and universal property establish the map rigorously. Conclude equality of image and kernel without claiming injectivity at the left.

items.title: The submodule $IM$ generated by products of elements of an ideal $I$ with elements of a module $M$
$M\otimes_RR/I\cong M/IM$ naturally
items.strategy: Tensor the exact sequence $I\to R\to R/I\to0$ with $M$ and use the tensor-unit isomorphism to identify the middle term with $M$. Track $i\otimes m$ to $im$ so that the incoming image is exactly $IM$, then apply the quotient universal property. Record both the $R$-module and induced $R/I$-module interpretations and include $I=0$ and $I=R$.

items.title: Flat and faithfully flat modules and ring homomorphisms
Flatness is equivalent to preserving injections and to the ideal and finitely generated ideal tests
items.strategy: Show exactness implies preservation of injections by adjoining cokernels, and that injection preservation implies both ideal tests. For the finitely generated-ideal converse, reduce a kernel element, represented by a finite tensor sum, to finitely generated submodules and then to an inclusion into a finite free module. Prove injectivity for submodules of $R^n$ by induction on $n$, with the ideal test as the base case. Track $n=0$ and the zero ideal explicitly.

items.title: Every projective module over a commutative ring is flat
items.strategy: First use arbitrary direct-sum distributivity and the tensor-unit isomorphism to show every free module is flat. A projective module is a direct summand of its canonical free cover; tensoring preserves the splitting maps, so its tensor functor is a direct summand of an exact free-module tensor functor and therefore preserves injections. No choice is needed for projective implies flat.

items.title: Under the stated choice boundary, free modules are projective and hence flat
items.strategy: Invoke the published theorem that arbitrary free modules are projective under AC, with finite bases needing only finite choice and the empty basis needing none, then apply projective implies flat. Also note that flatness of a free module follows directly from tensor-unit and arbitrary direct-sum distributivity without AC; keep the two logical routes distinct.

items.title: For flat $M$, one has $IM\cap JM=(I\cap J)M$
items.strategy: Apply flatness to the injection $I\cap J\to R$ inside the exact sequence $0\to I\cap J\to R\to R/I\oplus R/J$. Identify the tensor of $R$ with $M$, use the quotient-tensor isomorphisms to identify the two quotient components, and compute the resulting kernel as $IM\cap JM$. Check $I=R$, $J=R$, and the zero ideal.

items.title: A short exact sequence with flat quotient remains short exact after tensoring
items.strategy: For $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ with $C$ flat, resolve the other tensor factor by a free cover and form the resulting three-by-three diagram. Right exactness supplies the rows and columns, tensoring with the free module gives an exact middle row, and flatness of $C$ gives the required injective outer map. Perform the elementary diagram chase explicitly rather than naming an unbuilt snake lemma.

items.title: Restriction of scalars and extension of scalars $S\otimes_RM$ along a ring homomorphism $R\to S$
Extension of scalars is left adjoint to restriction of scalars
items.strategy: For a ring map $R\to S$, an $R$-module $M$, and an $S$-module $N$, send an $S$-linear map $S\otimes_RM\to N$ to $m\mapsto F(1\otimes m)$. Conversely send an $R$-linear map $f:M\to N$ to $s\otimes m\mapsto sf(m)$, verify balance, and invoke the universal property. Check the two maps inverse and natural in both modules.

items.title: Change of rings: $N\otimes_RM\cong N\otimes_S(S\otimes_RM)$
items.strategy: For $R\to S$, a right $S$-module $N$, and a left $R$-module $M$, specialize bimodule associativity to the $(S,R)$-bimodule $S$ and use $N\otimes_SS\cong N$. Track the isomorphism on elementary tensors as $n\otimes m\mapsto n\otimes(1\otimes m)$ and its inverse $n\otimes(s\otimes m)\mapsto ns\otimes m$.

items.title: Extension of scalars carries flat modules to flat modules
items.strategy: For $R\to S$ and flat $M$ over $R$, rewrite $N\otimes_S(S\otimes_RM)$ as $N\otimes_RM$ by change of rings for every injection of right $S$-modules. Restriction of scalars preserves injectivity, so flatness over $R$ gives injectivity after tensoring; conclude $S\otimes_RM$ is flat over $S$.

items.title: Flatness is transitive under a flat change of rings
items.strategy: Let $R\to S$ be flat and let $N$ be flat over $S$. For an exact sequence of $R$-modules, first tensor with $S$ to retain exactness, then tensor the resulting $S$-sequence with $N$. Use change-of-rings associativity and the tensor-unit map to identify the composite with tensoring directly by the restricted $R$-module $N$. State the corresponding composition result for flat ring maps.

items.title: The character dual of a flat module is injective
items.strategy: Let $R$ be commutative, let $P$ be flat, and let $D$ be an injective abelian group. Give $P^+=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(P,D)$ the action $(r\phi)(p)=\phi(rp)$. Establish the natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,P^+)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(M\otimes_RP,D)$. Flatness turns a module injection into an injection after tensoring, and injectivity of $D$ extends the corresponding group homomorphism; transpose back to prove $P^+$ injective.

items.title: False: $\mathbb Z/m\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n$ is nonzero for all positive $m,n$
items.strategy: Use the quotient-tensor theorem to identify the tensor product with $(\mathbb Z/m)/n(\mathbb Z/m)$, then use Bezout to identify this quotient with $\mathbb Z/\gcd(m,n)$. The concrete choice $(m,n)=(2,3)$ gives the zero group and refutes the claim. Treat the convention $\mathbb Z/1=0$ explicitly.

items.title: $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n=0$ for every positive $n$
items.strategy: Apply the quotient-tensor theorem with $M=\mathbb Q$ and $I=n\mathbb Z$. Multiplication by positive $n$ is surjective on $\mathbb Q$, so $n\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q$ and the quotient is zero. Do not use this statement at $n=0$.

items.title: $(R/I)\otimes_R(R/J)\cong R/(I+J)$ for ideals of a commutative ring
items.strategy: Apply the quotient-tensor theorem to $M=R/I$ and the ideal $J$. Identify $J(R/I)$ with $(I+J)/I$, and use the quotient-of-a-quotient isomorphism to obtain $R/(I+J)$. Include $I=R$, $J=R$, and both zero ideals.

items.title: $S\otimes_RR[x]\cong S[x]$ as $S$-algebras
items.strategy: For a homomorphism of commutative rings $R\to S$, send $s\otimes\sum_i r_ix^i$ to $\sum_i s f(r_i)x^i$. Descend the formula by the tensor universal property and verify multiplication using the tensor-product algebra law. Construct the inverse by sending each monomial coefficient $s x^i$ to $s\otimes x^i$ and use finite coefficient support to prove the composites are identities.

items.title: For a field extension $K/F$, one has $K\otimes_FM_n(F)\cong M_n(K)$ as $K$-algebras
items.strategy: Send $k\otimes(a_{ij})$ to $(k a_{ij})$ entrywise. The matrix units form an $F$-basis, so the tensor-basis theorem proves this is a $K$-module isomorphism; multiplication of matrix units proves it is a $K$-algebra isomorphism. Include $n=0$ under the library's empty-matrix convention and $n=1$ as the tensor-unit case.

items.title: For a field extension $K/F$, one has $K\otimes_FF^n\cong K^n$
items.strategy: Use extension of scalars together with the standard basis of $F^n$: the elements $1\otimes e_j$ form a $K$-basis by the product-basis theorem. Send $k\otimes(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})$ to $(ka_0,\ldots,ka_{n-1})$ and verify the inverse on the basis. Include $n=0$.

items.title: $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\cong\mathbb C\times\mathbb C$ as $\mathbb R$-algebras
items.strategy: Use the published real embedding and real basis $1,i$ of $\mathbb C$. Descend the bilinear map $z\otimes w\mapsto(zw,\overline z\,w)$, verify multiplicativity from the tensor-product algebra law, and compare the four real basis elements $1\otimes1$, $i\otimes1$, $1\otimes i$, $i\otimes i$ with their images to prove bijectivity. Exhibit the product idempotents as halves of $1\otimes1\mp i\otimes i$.

items.title: Tensoring the injection $k[x]\xrightarrow{\cdot x}k[x]$ with $k[x]/(x)$ gives the zero map
items.strategy: Multiplication by $x$ is injective because $k[x]$ is a domain. Identify each tensor product with $k[x]/(x)$ by the tensor-unit and quotient-tensor results. The induced map is multiplication by the class of $x$, hence zero, while the source is nonzero. This is the polynomial analogue of the integer counterexample.

items.title: False: $m\otimes n=0$ implies $m=0$ or $n=0$
items.strategy: In $\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/2$, the nonzero factors $2$ and $\overline1$ satisfy $2\otimes\overline1=1\otimes2\overline1=0$. Use the unit isomorphism to confirm that $\mathbb Z\otimes\mathbb Z/2$ itself is nonzero, so the witness is not caused by a zero tensor-product group.

items.title: False: every element of $M\otimes_RN$ is an elementary tensor
items.strategy: For any field $F$, take bases $e_1,e_2$ of $F^2$ and $f_1,f_2$ of another copy. The tensor $e_1\otimes f_1+e_2\otimes f_2$ has coefficient matrix of rank two. If it were $(ae_1+be_2)\otimes(cf_1+df_2)$, coefficient comparison would give $ac=bd=1$ and $ad=bc=0$, an immediate contradiction in a field.

items.title: False: tensoring preserves injections
items.strategy: Start with the injection $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\cdot2}\mathbb Z$. Tensor with $\mathbb Z/2$ and identify both sides with $\mathbb Z/2$ using the unit isomorphism. The induced map is multiplication by $2$, hence zero and not injective. Place it beside right exactness to show precisely why tensoring is not left exact in general.
